detective.q: Genesis 9 curses Ham and his descendants with dark skin.
detective.why: Genesis 9:25 curses Canaan, Ham's son, and says nothing about skin color. The racial reading was added many centuries later.

detective.q: In 1662 Virginia made a child enslaved or free according to the mother's status.
detective.why: Virginia's 1662 act (partus sequitur ventrem) is in the colony's statutes. It meant children of enslaved women, including those fathered by enslavers, were born enslaved.

detective.q: Margaret Sanger, founder of the group that became Planned Parenthood, supported eugenics.
detective.why: Her writings and speeches show it, and Planned Parenthood itself acknowledged it in 2020.

detective.q: Planned Parenthood was founded to exterminate Black Americans.
detective.why: The record does not support it. Sanger opposed abortion in her lifetime, and Planned Parenthood did not provide abortions until about 1970. The real, documented abuses are forced sterilizations by states and federal programs.

detective.q: After Bacon's Rebellion (1676), Virginia's leaders deliberately used race to divide poor white and Black workers.
detective.why: The laws that followed are documented. How deliberate the strategy was is debated by historians (see Edmund Morgan and his critics).

detective.q: The U.S. Public Health Service watched hundreds of Black men go untreated for syphilis for 40 years.
detective.why: The Tuskegee study ran from 1932 to 1972. A federal panel reviewed it, and President Clinton apologized in 1997.

detective.q: Modern American policing grew directly out of slave patrols.
detective.why: Slave patrols are well documented and shaped Southern policing. Northern departments also grew from other models, such as the London police, so how direct the line is remains debated.

detective.q: The Book of Enoch explains where the different races came from.
detective.why: 1 Enoch tells of fallen angels (the Watchers) and their giant children. It has no teaching about race. Some modern groups have built race myths on it.

detective.q: The Vatican formally repudiated the “Doctrine of Discovery” in 2023.
detective.why: Two Vatican departments issued a joint statement on March 30, 2023, rejecting the doctrine.

detective.q: Racism was a consequence of slavery, not its original cause.
detective.why: This was Eric Williams's argument in Capitalism and Slavery (1944). Many historians agree; others stress older prejudices that existed before Atlantic slavery.

modules.title: Before race: where the fear came from
modules.short: There is no ancient secret. Race was built, mostly between 1450 and 1700, to justify taking land and people, and the fear behind it was fear of losing power.
modules.intro: People often ask why the targeting of Black, Brown and Native people has lasted so long, and whether some forgotten origin explains it. The record gives a clearer answer: modern race is recent, it was written into law on purpose, and it has been defended by whatever argument was handy, including scripture and science.

sections.h: The ancient world sorted people differently
sections.label: documented
sections.body:
Slavery is ancient, but for most of history it was not based on skin color. Greeks, Romans, Egyptians, Africans, Arabs and Europeans enslaved people taken in war, sold for debt, or born to enslaved mothers, and enslaved people came from every region. The English word slave itself comes from Slav, because so many Eastern Europeans were enslaved in the Middle Ages.

Historian Frank Snowden showed that Greek and Roman writers described Africans with curiosity and sometimes admiration, without the idea of a fixed racial ranking.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
The idea that some people are naturally meant to be owned was spelled out step by step:

  • 1452–1455: Pope Nicholas V's bulls Dum Diversas and Romanus Pontifex authorized Portugal's king to conquer “Saracens and pagans” and reduce them to perpetual slavery. Portugal's African slave trade grew under them.
  • 1493: Inter caetera gave Spain lands “discovered” in the Americas. These bulls became the Doctrine of Discovery, which the U.S. Supreme Court adopted in Johnson v. M'Intosh (1823) to deny Native nations full ownership of their land. The Vatican repudiated the doctrine in 2023. The Supreme Court has not.
  • 1662: Virginia ruled that a child follows the condition of the mother, so children of enslaved women, including children of their enslavers, were born enslaved.
  • 1667–1705: Virginia declared that baptism does not free a slave (1667), that killing an enslaved person during “correction” was not a felony (1669), banned interracial marriage (1691), and gathered everything into the 1705 slave codes. France's Code Noir (1685) did the same for its colonies.

sections.label: debated
sections.body:
In 1676, Bacon's Rebellion brought white indentured servants and enslaved Africans together in an armed revolt against Virginia's government. In the decades that followed, Virginia's laws gave poor white people small privileges (freedom dues, the right to bear arms, the right to strike a Black person) while taking rights away from all Black people, free or enslaved.

That the laws changed is documented. Historian Edmund Morgan argued that the elite used race on purpose to keep poor white and Black people from uniting again. Others think the shift had more to do with the falling cost of enslaved Africans compared with English servants. Most agree the effect was the same.

sections.h: The practice came first, the ideas followed
sections.label: debated
sections.body:
In 1944 the Trinidadian historian Eric Williams wrote that “slavery was not born of racism: rather, racism was the consequence of slavery.” Ibram X. Kendi's Stamped from the Beginning (2016) traces the same pattern over five centuries: racist ideas were developed to defend policies that were already profitable.

Thomas Jefferson, who enslaved more than 600 people over his life, offered Black inferiority “as a suspicion only” in his Notes on the State of Virginia (1785). Within decades, “scientists” were measuring skulls to prove it (see the module on science).

sections.h: What the fear was really about
sections.label: documented
sections.body:
The fear was real. It was fear of revolt, of revenge, and of losing power at the ballot box:

  • Haiti, 1791–1804: enslaved people overthrew French rule and founded the first free Black republic. France later forced Haiti to pay 150 million francs (reduced to 90 million) for its own freedom, a debt Haiti paid off over about 120 years.
  • Nat Turner's rebellion, 1831: afterward, Virginia and other states tightened bans on teaching Black people to read and on Black preachers and gatherings.
  • Reconstruction, 1867–1877: Black men voted and held office, and South Carolina's lower house had a Black majority. White-supremacist violence ended it, including the 1898 coup in Wilmington, North Carolina, where an elected biracial government was overthrown by force.
  • “Replacement”: Madison Grant's The Passing of the Great Race (1916) warned that white Americans were being outbred. It helped pass the 1924 immigration quotas. The same fear, renamed the “Great Replacement,” was cited by the killers in El Paso (2019) and Buffalo (2022).

sections.h: How scripture was used, and misused
sections.label: documented
sections.body:
The “Curse of Ham.” In Genesis 9:20–27, Noah curses Canaan, Ham's son, to be a servant. The text says nothing about skin color or Africa. Linking the curse to dark skin came much later and was spread by interpreters across several traditions. By the 1800s it was a standard pro-slavery argument in American pulpits.

The “Slave Bible.” In 1807 a British missionary society printed Select Parts of the Holy Bible, for the Use of the Negro Slaves. It cut most of the Old Testament, including the Exodus story of freedom from slavery, and kept passages like “Servants, be obedient to them that are your masters.”

Scripture was also the strongest weapon against slavery: enslaved people sang of Moses and Exodus, and abolitionists from Frederick Douglass to the Black church built their case on it.

sections.h: The Book of Enoch and modern race myths
sections.label: belief
sections.body:
1 Enoch is an ancient Jewish book that is part of the Bible of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church; fragments were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and the Letter of Jude (verses 14–15) quotes it. It tells how angels called the Watchers came to earth, taught forbidden knowledge, and fathered giants (the Nephilim of Genesis 6). It contains no teaching about race.

Modern movements have still built race stories on Genesis and Enoch. We describe them so you can recognize them, not because they are true:

  • Christian Identity “two-seedline” theology, a white-supremacist doctrine claiming Jews and people of color descend from the serpent or from “pre-Adamic” races.
  • The Nation of Islam's story of Yakub, which teaches that a scientist named Yakub created white people thousands of years ago.
  • Some Hebrew Israelite groups teach that Black, Hispanic and Native Americans are the true Israelites and that others are cursed.

These stories mirror each other: each claims race is ancient, fixed and cosmic. The historical record shows the opposite: race is recent, made by people, and can be unmade.

modules.title: Columbus: what his own records say
modules.short: What Columbus wrote about the Taíno, enslavement and tribute on Hispaniola, his arrest in chains, the records about Africans sailing west before him, and the myths on all sides.
modules.intro: Columbus is usually taught as a discoverer. His own journal and letters, and the reports of the Spaniards who investigated him, tell a different story. They also contain intriguing passages about Africans and the Atlantic, which have been both ignored and exaggerated. Here is what the records actually say.
discuss: Why do you think Columbus was taught as a hero for so long?
What does it mean that the African-contact records exist but don't prove contact?
How should a town decide what to celebrate on the second Monday in October?

sections.h: Who he was, and what he already knew
sections.label: documented
sections.body:
Columbus was a Genoese sailor who sailed for the Crown of Castile in 1492 under a contract, the Capitulations of Santa Fe, that promised him a tenth of the wealth he found and the titles of admiral and governor. He was looking for a western route to Asia. Before that, he had sailed with the Portuguese to their fortress at São Jorge da Mina (Elmina) on the coast of present-day Ghana, the center of Portugal's trade in gold and enslaved Africans. He knew that trade firsthand.

His journal of the first voyage survives only as a summary made decades later by the friar Bartolomé de las Casas, partly quoting him and partly paraphrasing.

sections.h: What he wrote about the people he met
sections.label: documented
sections.body: On October 13, 1492, the journal describes the Lucayan (Taíno) people as “none of them black, but the color of the Canary Islanders.” On October 14 it says: “with fifty men they could all be subjugated and made to do whatever one might wish.” From the first days, he wrote about them as future servants and converts.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: In 1495 Columbus's men captured about 1,500 Taíno; around 500 were shipped to Spain to be sold, and about 200 died on the voyage (Michele da Cuneo's eyewitness account). He imposed a tribute: every Taíno over 14 had to deliver a set amount of gold every three months. Las Casas, who lived on the island, wrote that those who failed were brutally punished, including having their hands cut off. In 2006 historians published the report of Francisco de Bobadilla, sent by the Crown in 1500 to investigate; witnesses described Columbus and his brothers ordering mutilations, whippings and executions. Bobadilla sent Columbus back to Spain in chains. He was released but never again allowed to govern.

sections.label: debated
sections.body: Estimates of Hispaniola's population in 1492 range from about 100,000 to several million, and historians disagree sharply. A Spanish count in 1514 found only about 26,000 Taíno under forced labor; smallpox arrived in 1518. The collapse from violence, forced labor, famine and disease is documented; the starting number is debated. The Taíno did not vanish: genetic studies find substantial Taíno ancestry in Puerto Ricans and others today, and Taíno communities are reviving their culture.

sections.h: Africans sailing west: what the records actually say
sections.label: debated
sections.body:
Several real documents raise the question of whether Africans crossed the Atlantic before 1492:

  • Columbus, third voyage (1498): in Las Casas's summary, Columbus says he sailed southwest partly to test King João II of Portugal's belief that there was land to the southwest, and that “canoes had been found which set out from the coast of Guinea [West Africa] and sailed to the west with merchandise.”
  • Reports of “black people” and guanín: the same accounts report that people on Hispaniola spoke of Black traders who had come from the south and southeast with spear points of guanín, a gold-copper alloy; guanín was also a Taíno word and material.
  • Panama, 1513: chronicler Peter Martyr wrote that Balboa's expedition met Black people at Quarequá, whom he guessed had come by sea from “Ethiopia.”
  • Mali, about 1311: the scholar al-ʿUmarī recorded Mansa Musa saying that his predecessor (usually called Abu Bakr II) sent fleets into the Atlantic and then sailed himself, never to return.

Historian Ivan Van Sertima's They Came Before Columbus (1976) built on these to argue Africans reached the Americas. Most archaeologists and historians conclude the case is unproven: no African settlement, artifact or pre-1492 African ancestry has been found in the Americas, and claims that the Olmec stone heads show Africans are rejected by Mesoamerican specialists and many Indigenous scholars, who see them as taking credit from Native peoples. The documents are real; what they prove is debated.

sections.h: “African villages were already here when Columbus arrived”
sections.label: belief
sections.body:
Columbus's journal and letters don't describe African villages. They describe the Taíno, whom he said were “none of them black.” The first Africans documented in the Americas came with the Spanish: free Africans such as the conquistador Juan Garrido, and enslaved Africans, whom the Crown allowed to be shipped to Hispaniola from 1501. Enslaved Africans led one of the first revolts in the Americas there in 1521.

The idea that Africans came first grew partly as a response to centuries of racist claims that Africa had no history (the philosopher Hegel wrote in the 1830s that Africa was “no historical part of the world”). The documented record answers those claims on its own: the Mali Empire and Timbuktu's manuscripts, Great Zimbabwe (which colonial authorities falsely claimed others had built), and the Benin bronzes looted by British troops in 1897, some of which have now been returned.

sections.h: Columbus Day and Indigenous Peoples' Day
sections.label: documented
sections.body: President Benjamin Harrison proclaimed a one-time Columbus celebration in 1892, months after a mob in New Orleans lynched 11 Italian Americans; for Italian Americans facing discrimination, Columbus became a symbol of belonging. It became a federal holiday in 1937. South Dakota renamed the day Native American Day in 1990, Berkeley adopted Indigenous Peoples' Day in 1992, and many states and cities have followed. Presidential proclamations have changed with administrations.

modules.title: The colonizers: Portugal, Spain, Britain and the empire system
modules.short: How Portugal opened the Atlantic slave trade, Spain debated whether Native people were human, Britain built the plantation law the U.S. inherited, and the United States became an empire itself.
modules.intro: Columbus was one person in a system that ran for four centuries. Each empire added a piece of the machinery: the trade, the legal theory, the plantation code, the racial categories. Together they built the world the CAREN Act is still responding to.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: In 1444, at Lagos in Portugal, about 235 captive Africans were divided and sold in a public square, an event the royal chronicler Gomes Eanes de Zurara described in detail. Portugal built Elmina castle in 1482 and traded along the African coast. In 1526, King Afonso I of Kongo, himself a Christian ally of Portugal, wrote to Portugal's king protesting that traders were kidnapping his people, “even noblemen and the sons of noblemen.” Portuguese and Brazilian ships carried about 5.8 million Africans across the Atlantic, more than any other nation. Brazil was the largest destination and the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888.

sections.h: Spain asks whether Native people are fully human
sections.label: documented
sections.body: From 1513, Spanish conquistadors read the Requerimiento aloud, in Spanish, to people who couldn't understand it, demanding submission to the Crown and the Church, and declaring that any resulting deaths were their own fault. Native people were assigned to Spaniards as forced laborers under the encomienda. Bartolomé de las Casas, a former encomendero turned friar, spent fifty years denouncing it; the New Laws of 1542 limited it. At the Valladolid debate (1550–51), Las Casas argued against Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda, who claimed, citing Aristotle, that Native people were “natural slaves.” Spain's colonies later sorted people into dozens of mixed-ancestry castas, recorded in official paintings.

sections.label: debated
sections.body: Some historians trace modern race to Spain's limpieza de sangre (“purity of blood”) statutes, which from the 1400s barred people with Jewish or Muslim ancestors from offices even after conversion, making ancestry, not belief, the test. Others see race emerging mainly from Atlantic slavery and English colonial law. Most agree it formed between about 1450 and 1700, which is the argument of the module “Before race.”

sections.label: documented
sections.body: John Hawkins led England's first slaving voyages in the 1560s, later with Queen Elizabeth I's backing. The Royal African Company, chartered under the future James II, shipped more enslaved Africans than any other single company; many were branded with “DY” for the Duke of York. Barbados's 1661 slave code became the model for Jamaica's and South Carolina's. British ships carried about 3.2 million Africans in all. In 1781 the crew of the slave ship Zong threw about 130 captives overboard, and the owners sued their insurers for the loss as “cargo.” The first Africans in English Virginia arrived in 1619 aboard the White Lion, an English privateer that had seized them from a Portuguese ship carrying captives from Angola.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: The Dutch West India Company traded enslaved Africans to the Americas and used enslaved labor in New Amsterdam (New York). France's Code Noir (1685) governed its colonies; Saint-Domingue, today's Haiti, became the most profitable colony in the world on the labor of enslaved Africans, until they overthrew the French (see “Before race” and “A world system”).

sections.h: The United States becomes an empire
sections.label: documented
sections.body: In 1893, American businessmen backed by U.S. Marines overthrew Hawaii's Queen Liliʻuokalani; Congress formally apologized in 1993. After 1898 the U.S. took Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines. Rudyard Kipling's poem “The White Man's Burden” (1899) urged Americans to rule the Philippines, where a war against independence fighters killed hundreds of thousands of Filipinos by most estimates. In the Insular Cases (1901) the Supreme Court called Puerto Rico “foreign … in a domestic sense”; its residents are U.S. citizens who still can't vote for president.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Across five centuries and every empire, the same tools appear: claim the land (discovery), classify people by ancestry or color, take their labor, write it into law, justify it with religion and then science, and divide the colonized from one another. Resistance appears everywhere too, from Kongo's king to Haiti's revolutionaries to Hawaii's queen. The rest of the Learn modules follow these tools into American institutions.

modules.title: Discovery and conquest
modules.short: How the Doctrine of Discovery became U.S. law, and what it did to Native nations: war, removal, allotment and boarding schools, and the fight for sovereignty today.
modules.intro: Before there was a color line in North America, there was a land line. The idea that Christian Europeans could claim lands already lived on became U.S. law, and every Native nation lived with the consequences.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Hundreds of nations with their own governments, trade networks and cities lived here. Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, had perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 people around 1100 CE. Disease, war and enslavement followed contact; by 1900 the U.S. census counted only about 237,000 Native people. Historian Andrés Reséndez estimates that 2.5 to 5 million Native people were enslaved across the Americas between 1492 and 1900, a figure that is still debated.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: In Johnson v. M'Intosh (1823) the Supreme Court held that “discovery” gave the U.S. title to Native land. In Worcester v. Georgia (1832) it ruled that Georgia had no authority over Cherokee land, but President Jackson's government enforced the Indian Removal Act (1830) anyway. The Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Muscogee (Creek) and Seminole nations were forced west; thousands of Cherokee died on the Trail of Tears in 1838–39. Some of these nations had adopted slavery, and enslaved Black people were forced along the same trails.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: At Sand Creek, Colorado, in 1864, U.S. volunteers killed more than 150 Cheyenne and Arapaho people, most of them women, children and elders, at a camp flying a U.S. flag. At Wounded Knee in 1890, soldiers killed about 250 or more Lakota. In California, Governor Peter Burnett declared in 1851 that “a war of extermination will continue to be waged”; state-funded militias killed thousands, and the Native population fell from about 150,000 to about 30,000 between 1846 and 1870. In 2019 California's governor apologized and called it genocide.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: The Dawes Act (1887) broke reservations into individual plots and sold the “surplus.” Native-held land fell from about 138 million acres in 1887 to about 48 million by 1934. In the 1950s, “termination” policy ended federal recognition of more than 100 tribes, and the Relocation program moved Native families to cities with promises of jobs that often didn't exist.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: “Kill the Indian in him, and save the man,” said Richard Henry Pratt, who founded the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in 1879. The federal government ran or supported 408 boarding schools that took children from their families, banned their languages and religions, and used harsh discipline. The Interior Department's investigation documented at least 973 deaths of children (2024). In October 2024 President Biden formally apologized.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Native activists occupied Alcatraz (1969–71) and Wounded Knee (1973), and won the Indian Self-Determination Act (1975). In McGirt v. Oklahoma (2020) the Supreme Court held that much of eastern Oklahoma remains Muscogee (Creek) reservation for purposes of federal criminal law. The protests at Standing Rock (2016) drew thousands of supporters, and in 2021 Deb Haaland (Laguna Pueblo) became the first Native American cabinet secretary.

modules.title: Slavery makes race law
modules.short: The Atlantic slave trade, the national economy it built, the laws that made slavery permanent and hereditary, and the people who resisted.
modules.intro: Slavery in America was not a Southern side story. It was written into the Constitution, financed by Northern banks, and was the country's largest financial asset by 1860.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: About 12.5 million Africans were forced onto slave ships between the 1500s and 1866, and about 10.7 million survived the Middle Passage (SlaveVoyages.org). About 388,000 were brought directly to mainland North America. After Congress banned importing enslaved people in 1808, a domestic trade forcibly moved about a million people from the Upper South to the cotton fields of the Deep South, tearing families apart.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: By 1860, about 3.95 million people were enslaved in the U.S. Their market value as “property” was greater than that of all the country's railroads and factories combined. Cotton grown by enslaved people made up more than half of U.S. exports. Northern banks took enslaved people as loan collateral, insurers wrote policies on their lives, and universities profited: in 1838 the Jesuits who ran Georgetown sold 272 people to keep the college afloat.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: The Constitution counted enslaved people as three-fifths of a person for representation, protected the slave trade until 1808, and required escaped people to be returned. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 forced free states to help capture them. In Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) Chief Justice Taney wrote that Black people had “no rights which the white man was bound to respect.”

sections.label: debated
sections.body: Historian Edward Baptist (The Half Has Never Been Told, 2014) argued that rising cotton-picking rates came largely from systematic torture and quotas. Economists Alan Olmstead and Paul Rhode answered that better cotton varieties explain most of the gain. Both sides agree enslaved people were whipped, sold and separated from their families; the debate is over how much violence drove productivity.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Enslaved people resisted every day, by slowing work, escaping and rebelling: Stono (1739), the German Coast uprising (1811), Nat Turner (1831). Harriet Tubman made about 13 trips back into Maryland and led about 70 people to freedom. Maroon communities lived in places like the Great Dismal Swamp. About 179,000 Black men served in the Union Army. On June 19, 1865, Union troops announced emancipation in Galveston, Texas; Juneteenth became a federal holiday in 2021.

modules.title: Reconstruction overthrown
modules.short: Freedom, citizenship and Black political power after the Civil War, and the terror, court rulings and laws that took them away.
modules.intro: For about a decade after the Civil War, the United States tried to become a multiracial democracy. How that effort was destroyed explains much of the century that followed.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: The 13th Amendment (1865) ended slavery, the 14th (1868) made everyone born here a citizen with “equal protection of the laws,” and the 15th (1870) barred race discrimination in voting. The Freedmen's Bureau helped found schools across the South. About 2,000 Black men held office, including 16 members of Congress such as Senators Hiram Revels and Blanche K. Bruce and Representative Robert Smalls. Reconstruction legislatures created the South's first public school systems.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: The Ku Klux Klan formed in 1865–66. White mobs killed dozens of Black people in Memphis and New Orleans in 1866, and as many as 150 at Colfax in 1873. Congress passed the Enforcement Acts and the Ku Klux Klan Act (1870–71), and President Grant sent troops and suspended habeas corpus in nine South Carolina counties. For a time, it worked.

sections.h: The courts and Congress walk away
sections.label: documented
sections.body: The Supreme Court narrowed the 14th Amendment in the Slaughter-House Cases (1873), freed the Colfax killers in U.S. v. Cruikshank (1876), and struck down the Civil Rights Act of 1875 in the Civil Rights Cases (1883). In Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) it approved “separate but equal.”

sections.label: debated
sections.body: After the disputed 1876 election, Rutherford B. Hayes became president and federal troops stopped protecting Reconstruction governments in the South. Historians debate whether a formal deal was struck or the outcome reflected a broader Northern retreat. The result is not debated: Southern states were left to white “Redeemer” governments.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: States passed segregation laws and stripped Black voting rights (see the module on the vote). EJI documented more than 4,400 racial terror lynchings from 1877 to 1950. Ida B. Wells exposed the lie that lynching punished crime in Southern Horrors (1892). Congress failed to pass an anti-lynching law for more than a century, until the Emmett Till Antilynching Act was signed in 2022. About 6 million Black Southerners left in the Great Migration (1910–1970).

sections.label: belief
sections.body: The claim that the Civil War was about states' rights or tariffs rather than slavery spread after the war through textbooks, monuments and films. The secession documents say otherwise. Mississippi's declared: “Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery.” Most Confederate monuments were put up between about 1900 and the 1920s, and again in the 1950s and 1960s, during Jim Crow and the civil rights movement, not right after the war.

modules.title: What we built: Black towns, institutions and self-determination
modules.short: All-Black towns, banks, insurance companies, newspapers, churches and colleges built after slavery, often the very places that were later attacked.
modules.intro: This history is not only about what was done to Black Americans. Within a generation of slavery, Black communities built towns, banks, schools and businesses from almost nothing. Knowing what was built explains what was lost, and shows the model for rebuilding.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: After Reconstruction, Black families founded their own towns where they could own land, vote and govern themselves. Oklahoma alone had more than 50, the most of any state, including Boley (founded 1903). Others include Nicodemus, Kansas (1877, now a National Historic Site); Eatonville, Florida (1887, one of the first incorporated Black towns and Zora Neale Hurston's hometown); Mound Bayou, Mississippi (1887, founded by Isaiah Montgomery, who had been enslaved); and Allensworth, California (1908, founded by Colonel Allen Allensworth, now a state historic park).

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Greenwood in Tulsa was the most famous, but not the only one. Durham's Parrish Street was home to North Carolina Mutual Life Insurance (1898), for decades the largest Black-owned business in America. In Richmond's Jackson Ward, Maggie L. Walker founded the St. Luke Penny Savings Bank in 1903, the first bank chartered by a woman in the United States. Atlanta's Auburn Avenue had Atlanta Life Insurance, founded by Alonzo Herndon, who was born enslaved. (See the module on communities destroyed.)

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Free Black Philadelphians formed the Free African Society, a mutual-aid group, in 1787, and Richard Allen founded the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816. The first Black newspaper, Freedom's Journal, began in 1827; the Chicago Defender later helped drive the Great Migration. Cheyney University (1837) is the oldest HBCU. The Negro Motorist Green Book (1936–1966) guided Black travelers to safe hotels, restaurants and gas stations in a country full of sundown towns.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Ida B. Wells documented lynching and urged Black families to leave Memphis and buy guns for self-defense. Fannie Lou Hamer founded the Freedom Farm Cooperative in 1969 so Black families in Mississippi could grow their own food and own land. The Black Panther Party's Free Breakfast for Children program (1969) fed thousands of children every day and is often credited with pushing the federal government to expand school breakfasts.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Many of these places were attacked precisely because they succeeded (see the modules on communities destroyed and on evidence of performance, where economist Lisa Cook shows how violence suppressed Black invention). The model they used still works: own land, bank together, build institutions, and teach the next generation. Black Americans founded more than 130 banks between 1888 and 1934; only about 20 remain today. Supporting them is one of the quests.

modules.title: Faith: used to oppress, used to liberate
modules.short: How scripture justified slavery and how the Black church, abolitionists and people of many faiths turned it into a force for freedom.
modules.intro: Religion has been on both sides of this history. The same Bible that was cut down into a “Slave Bible” carried the Exodus story that enslaved people sang about.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Many enslavers controlled worship, but enslaved people met secretly in “hush harbors” to pray and sing their own way. In the 1790s Richard Allen and Absalom Jones walked out of Philadelphia's St. George's Methodist Church after being pulled from their knees during prayer for sitting in the “wrong” section; Allen went on to found the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816.

sections.label: debated
sections.body: Spirituals spoke of crossing Jordan and reaching the promised land, and many listeners heard freedom in them. The popular claim that specific songs like “Follow the Drinking Gourd” were coded maps for the Underground Railroad is debated; historians have found little evidence that song was known before the 1920s. The broader point, that faith sustained resistance, is well documented.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Quakers in Germantown, Pennsylvania, issued one of the first protests against slavery in 1688. Frederick Douglass drew a sharp line between “the Christianity of this land” and “the Christianity of Christ.” Nat Turner understood his rebellion as a religious calling.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Ministers founded the Southern Christian Leadership Conference in 1957, and churches served as meeting halls, schools and sanctuaries, which made them targets: the 1963 bombing of Birmingham's 16th Street Baptist Church killed four girls, and in 2015 a white supremacist murdered nine worshippers at Charleston's Emanuel AME Church. People of other faiths marched too: Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel said that at Selma he felt his legs were praying. Malcolm X's 1964 pilgrimage to Mecca changed how he saw race.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Congregations run “Souls to the Polls” voting drives, food pantries and reentry programs, and the revived Poor People's Campaign (2018) organizes across faiths. Faith communities are natural hosts for teach-ins and coalitions.

modules.title: Black veterans: fighting for a country that fought them
modules.short: From the Revolution to Vietnam: Black soldiers who fought abroad and were attacked at home, and how a veteran's blinding helped desegregate the military.
modules.intro: Black Americans have served in every U.S. war. Many came home expecting the freedom they had fought for, and that expectation made them targets.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Crispus Attucks, a man of African and Native descent, was the first killed in the Boston Massacre (1770). Thousands of Black soldiers fought for independence, while others joined the British, who promised freedom to people enslaved by rebels. In the Civil War, about 179,000 Black men served in the Union Army. Confederates massacred surrendering Black soldiers at Fort Pillow in 1864.

sections.h: World War I and the backlash
sections.label: documented
sections.body: The 369th Infantry, the “Harlem Hellfighters,” spent more time in combat than almost any other American unit. At home, the Army hanged 19 Black soldiers of the 24th Infantry after the 1917 Houston riot, 13 of them in a single day without appeal; in 2023 the Army set aside the convictions of 110 of the soldiers. After the war, Black veterans were beaten and lynched, some in uniform, during the Red Summer of 1919 (EJI, Targeting Black Veterans).

sections.label: documented
sections.body: More than a million Black Americans served in World War II, including the Tuskegee Airmen. The Pittsburgh Courier's “Double V” campaign called for victory over fascism abroad and racism at home. In 1944 an explosion at Port Chicago, California, killed 320 men, most of them Black sailors loading ammunition; 50 who refused to return to the same unsafe work were convicted of mutiny. The Navy exonerated them in 2024.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: In February 1946, hours after his honorable discharge, Sergeant Isaac Woodard was pulled off a bus in Batesburg, South Carolina, and beaten by the police chief until he was blind. An all-white jury acquitted the chief. Outrage over the case helped move President Truman to order the desegregation of the armed forces in 1948 (Executive Order 9981). Many civil rights leaders, including Medgar Evers, were veterans; Tulsa's defenders in 1921 were veterans too.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: No Black soldier received the Medal of Honor for World War II until 1997, when seven were finally awarded it after a review; only one, Vernon Baker, was still alive. Black veterans were also largely shut out of the GI Bill's benefits (see the module on wealth).

modules.title: Science as a weapon: medicine, eugenics and reproductive control
modules.short: Scientific racism, medical experiments, and the forced sterilization of tens of thousands of Americans, plus what the evidence does and doesn't show about Planned Parenthood.
modules.intro: When religion could no longer justify slavery and segregation, science was asked to. This module covers what was done in medicine's name, much of it within living memory, and separates the documented record from claims that go beyond it.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: In 1758 Carl Linnaeus divided humans into varieties and gave each a temperament: Europeans “governed by laws,” Africans “governed by caprice.” In the 1830s–40s Samuel Morton measured skull sizes to rank races, and in 1854 Josiah Nott and George Gliddon's Types of Mankind argued the races were separate species, a book widely used to defend slavery. None of it holds up: modern genetics finds more variation within any so-called race than between them.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
• J. Marion Sims, 1845–1849: the “father of modern gynecology” developed his surgery by operating repeatedly, without anesthesia, on enslaved women including Anarcha, Betsey and Lucy. New York City removed his Central Park statue in 2018.
  • Tuskegee, 1932–1972: the U.S. Public Health Service followed about 600 Black men in Alabama, 399 of them with syphilis, without telling them their diagnosis and without treating them, even after penicillin became the standard cure in the 1940s. It ended only when a whistleblower went to the press. President Clinton apologized in 1997.
  • Henrietta Lacks, 1951: cells taken from her cancer without her knowledge became the HeLa line used in labs worldwide. Her family reached a settlement with one company in 2023.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
In Buck v. Bell (1927) the Supreme Court upheld forced sterilization (“Three generations of imbeciles are enough”). It has never been overruled. More than 60,000 people were sterilized under laws in 32 states. Early victims were mostly poor white people labeled “feebleminded”; after the 1950s, in the South especially, they were increasingly Black women.

  • North Carolina's Eugenics Board sterilized about 7,600 people from 1929 to 1974. In 2013 it became the first state to pay survivors.
  • Fannie Lou Hamer was sterilized without consent in 1961 while having a tumor removed. She called it a “Mississippi appendectomy,” a common experience among Black women in the South.
  • The Relf sisters, ages 12 and 14, were sterilized at a federally funded clinic in Montgomery, Alabama, in 1973. Their lawsuit led to federal consent rules.
  • Native women: a 1976 federal audit (GAO) found 3,406 sterilizations by the Indian Health Service in just four of its twelve areas from 1973 to 1976, many with inadequate consent.
  • Puerto Rico: by 1965 about a third of mothers had been sterilized, under programs encouraged by U.S. and island officials.
  • California sterilized about 20,000 people from 1909 to 1979, and nearly 150 women in state prisons from 2006 to 2010; a 2014 state audit found consent rules were broken.
  • Immigration detention: a 2022 bipartisan U.S. Senate investigation found that women at the Irwin County center in Georgia underwent excessive and often unnecessary gynecological procedures.

sections.label: debated
sections.body:
Margaret Sanger founded the American Birth Control League in 1921, which became Planned Parenthood in 1942. She supported eugenics, as many Progressive-era reformers did, and spoke to a women's auxiliary of the Ku Klux Klan in 1926. In 2020 Planned Parenthood of Greater New York removed her name from its Manhattan clinic over her eugenics ties.

In 1939 her federation started the “Negro Project” to bring birth control to the rural South. W.E.B. Du Bois and Mary McLeod Bethune supported it. In a letter about it, Sanger wrote: “We do not want word to go out that we want to exterminate the Negro population, and the minister is the man who can straighten out that idea if it ever occurs to any of their more rebellious members.” Historians disagree about that sentence. Most read it as worry that rumors would sink the project, not as a secret plan; critics read it as revealing.

sections.h: “Planned Parenthood was founded to exterminate Black Americans”
sections.label: belief
sections.body:
This claim, common in political campaigns, goes beyond the record. Sanger opposed abortion in her lifetime; she promoted contraception. Planned Parenthood did not provide abortions until about 1970. The documented coercion against Black, Native and Latina women came mainly from state eugenics boards and government-funded programs, not from a hidden plan inside one organization.

This site takes no position on abortion. It documents coercion: anyone, on any side, who wants to end it should know where it actually happened.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
CDC abortion surveillance reports show the abortion rate among Black women is roughly four times the rate among white women. Research from the CDC and the Guttmacher Institute links this to higher rates of unintended pregnancy, which in turn follow from unequal access to contraception and health care, from poverty, and from well-earned distrust of the medical system.

The same unequal system shows up elsewhere: Black women die from pregnancy-related causes at about two and a half to three times the rate of white women (CDC), a gap that holds even for college-educated women.

modules.title: Health: segregated care and false beliefs about bodies
modules.short: Segregated hospitals, myths about pain and skin, race “corrections” in medical formulas, COVID, and the toll of living with racism.
modules.intro: The medical abuses in the module on science are not the whole story. Everyday care has also been shaped by segregation and by false beliefs that Black bodies are different.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: The Hill-Burton Act (1946) funded hospital construction and explicitly allowed “separate but equal” facilities. A federal court struck that down in Simkins v. Moses H. Cone Memorial Hospital (1963). Medicare, launched in 1966, finished the job: hospitals had to integrate to get paid, and about a thousand did so within months.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: A 2016 study in PNAS found that about half of the white medical students and residents surveyed believed at least one false claim about biological differences, such as Black people having thicker skin, and those who did rated Black patients' pain lower. Pulse oximeters overestimate blood oxygen in patients with darker skin (New England Journal of Medicine, 2020), which can delay treatment. Medical groups have removed race “corrections” from the kidney function formula (2021) and lung function tests (2023).

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Black Americans' life expectancy has been several years shorter than white Americans', about five years in recent CDC data. During COVID-19, Black, Hispanic and Native Americans were hospitalized and died at higher rates than white Americans (CDC). Black maternal mortality is covered in the module on science.

sections.h: Weathering, and doctors who look like you
sections.label: debated
sections.body: Public health researcher Arline Geronimus proposed in 1992 that the chronic stress of facing racism “weathers” bodies, causing earlier illness. Many studies support the idea; the exact biological pathways are still debated. A 2020 study found Black newborns were more likely to survive when cared for by Black doctors; a 2024 reanalysis argued the effect mostly disappears after accounting for very low birth weight. Both studies are serious; the question isn't settled.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: More Black doctors, nurses and midwives; community health workers and doulas; insurance coverage; and removing race-based shortcuts from clinical tools. Health professionals can give their skills through the pro bono quests.

modules.title: Borders: who gets to be American
modules.short: “Free white persons,” Chinese Exclusion, racial quotas, mass deportations of Mexican Americans, Japanese American incarceration, and today's enforcement.
modules.intro: Immigration law has always been a way of deciding who counts as American. For most of U.S. history, it did so openly by race.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: The first Naturalization Act (1790) limited citizenship by naturalization to “free white persons.” Courts then had to decide who was white. In Ozawa (1922) the Supreme Court ruled a Japanese immigrant was not; in Thind (1923) it ruled that an Indian Sikh immigrant was not either, even though anthropologists classed him as “Caucasian.” Racial bars to naturalization weren't fully removed until 1952.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: The Page Act (1875) effectively barred Chinese women, and the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) barred Chinese laborers, the first U.S. law to exclude a group by nationality. It wasn't repealed until 1943. Chinese immigrants were held and interrogated at Angel Island in San Francisco Bay (1910–1940).

sections.label: documented
sections.body: The Immigration Act of 1924 set quotas based on the national origins of the U.S. population in 1890, to favor Northern Europeans, and barred almost all immigration from Asia. Eugenicists testified in its favor. The quota system lasted until the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: During the Depression (1929–1936), federal, state and local officials pushed out hundreds of thousands of Mexicans and Mexican Americans; estimates range from about 400,000 to more than a million, and many were U.S. citizens, including children. California apologized in 2005. During World War II the Bracero program recruited Mexican workers; in 1954 “Operation Wetback” carried out mass deportations. The government claimed over a million removals that year; historians consider that number inflated.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Executive Order 9066 (February 1942) led to the forced removal of about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry from the West Coast, two-thirds of them U.S. citizens, to camps behind barbed wire. The Supreme Court upheld it in Korematsu (1944). The Civil Liberties Act of 1988 apologized and paid $20,000 to each surviving person who had been incarcerated, and in 2018 the Court said Korematsu “was gravely wrong the day it was decided.”

sections.label: documented
sections.body: In 2018 the “zero tolerance” policy separated thousands of children from their parents at the border. Immigration detention holds tens of thousands of people on a given day. In September 2025 the Supreme Court allowed immigration agents in the Los Angeles area to resume stops that a lower court had found relied on factors including apparent ethnicity, language and type of work, while the case continues. A CAREN-style law protects anyone, citizen or not, from being reported to police in order to discriminate.

modules.title: Place: who gets to live where
modules.short: Racial zoning, covenants, redlining, sundown towns, blockbusting and the Fair Housing Act, and why neighborhoods are still divided.
modules.intro: Most American neighborhoods didn't become segregated by accident or by choice alone. Governments drew the lines, and many of those lines are still visible on the map.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Baltimore passed the first citywide racial zoning law in 1910; the Supreme Court struck racial zoning down in Buchanan v. Warley (1917). Developers and neighbors turned to racial covenants written into deeds, which the Court let stand in 1926. In Shelley v. Kraemer (1948) it ruled courts couldn't enforce them, but the language remains in millions of deeds. Some states, such as Minnesota (2019), now let owners formally strike it. The map's covenants layer shows more than 100,000 of them.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: From 1935 to 1940 the federal Home Owners' Loan Corporation graded neighborhoods in about 200 cities; Black and immigrant neighborhoods were colored red as “hazardous.” The Federal Housing Administration refused to insure loans in or near Black neighborhoods and recommended covenants. In Detroit in 1941, a developer built a half-mile wall to separate a new white subdivision from a Black neighborhood so the FHA would back its loans. Studies find formerly redlined areas today are poorer, have lower life expectancy, and run several degrees hotter in summer.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Historian James Loewen documented hundreds of towns that kept Black residents out after dark, by sign, ordinance or violence (see the old laws tracker). As Black families moved north and into new neighborhoods, real estate agents practiced “blockbusting,” scaring white owners into selling cheaply and reselling to Black families at a markup. The Fair Housing Act passed on April 11, 1968, a week after Martin Luther King Jr. was killed.

sections.h: Does zoning still keep neighborhoods apart?
sections.label: debated
sections.body: Explicit racial rules are illegal, but zoning that allows only single-family homes on large lots raises the price of entry to many neighborhoods. Researchers broadly agree such rules preserve economic segregation; they debate how much they preserve racial segregation today, compared with income differences, preferences and discrimination by landlords and lenders, which fair-housing tests still find.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Look up your neighborhood on the redlining and covenant layers. If your deed has a covenant and your state allows it, have it struck. Support fair-housing testing, inclusive zoning reform and down-payment help for first-time buyers in formerly redlined areas. (See also the modules on wealth and on communities destroyed.)

modules.title: Burned, flooded and taken: the communities America destroyed
modules.short: Black Wall Street in Tulsa and dozens of other Black, Brown and immigrant communities that were burned, driven out, flooded, seized or bulldozed, plus how gentrification continues the pattern.
modules.intro: Again and again, when Black communities built wealth, voted or simply grew, they were attacked: burned by mobs, driven off their land, flooded for dams, seized for parks and beaches, or bulldozed for highways. Each loss wiped out homes and businesses that would have passed wealth down to the next generation. This module tells those stories, and they are all on the map.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
In the early 1900s, Greenwood was home to about 10,000 Black residents. Its main street had hotels, theaters, groceries, doctors' and lawyers' offices, churches, two newspapers and a hospital. Oklahoma's segregation laws kept Black dollars inside the district, and they circulated there. Booker T. Washington is credited with calling it the “Negro Wall Street.” O.W. Gurley, J.B. Stradford and other Black entrepreneurs built it on land they owned.

May 31–June 1, 1921. A Black teenager, Dick Rowland, was arrested after a white elevator operator accused him of assault. A newspaper story inflamed the city. Black World War I veterans went to the courthouse to stop a lynching, and a white mob, many of them deputized by officials, invaded Greenwood. Over about 18 hours they burned 35 city blocks, including about 1,256 homes. The 2001 Oklahoma commission found that airplanes were used in the attack and estimated that 100 to 300 people were killed. About 6,000 Black residents were held in internment camps.

Afterward. Insurance companies denied claims under “riot” clauses, and the city tried to rezone the burned district so it couldn't be rebuilt. No one was ever prosecuted. Residents rebuilt anyway. Then, in the 1960s and 1970s, urban renewal and Interstate 244 cut through Greenwood again.

Still unresolved. The 2001 state commission recommended reparations; none have been paid by the state. Searches for mass graves at Oaklawn Cemetery began in 2020, and in 2024 one set of remains was identified as C.L. Daniel, a World War I veteran. Also in 2024, the Oklahoma Supreme Court dismissed the last survivors' lawsuit. In January 2025 the U.S. Justice Department called the massacre a civil rights crime of unparalleled magnitude, but said no one left alive could be prosecuted.

sections.h: Burned: a pattern, not an accident
sections.label: documented
sections.body:
Tulsa was one of many. The death tolls below are estimates, and many are disputed because officials undercounted. The pattern is clear: a mob, often set off by an accusation against a Black man or by Black voting, organizing or success, followed by fire.

  • Colfax, Louisiana, 1873: an estimated 62–153 Black men killed defending a courthouse after an election. The Supreme Court then let the killers go (U.S. v. Cruikshank, 1876).
  • Wilmington, North Carolina, 1898: the only successful coup on U.S. soil. The Black newspaper was burned and at least 60 people were killed.
  • Atlanta 1906, Springfield 1908, Slocum 1910: each sparked by rumors or accusations. Springfield led directly to the founding of the NAACP.
  • East St. Louis, 1917: about 6,000 people left homeless after white workers attacked Black workers.
  • Red Summer, 1919: violence in more than two dozen cities. In Elaine, Arkansas, Black sharecroppers trying to form a union were massacred, with estimates from about 100 to several hundred dead.
  • Ocoee, Florida, 1920: Black residents tried to vote. The entire Black community was burned out.
  • Rosewood, Florida, 1923: a white woman's accusation led to a whole town being burned. In 1994 Florida became the first state to pay reparations for racial violence.
  • Philadelphia, 1985: police dropped a bomb on the MOVE house; 11 people died, including 5 children, and 61 homes in a Black neighborhood burned.

Chinese immigrants were attacked the same way: in Los Angeles in 1871, in Rock Springs, Wyoming, in 1885, and in Tacoma, Washington, which expelled its entire Chinese population that year.

The link to today is direct. Many of these attacks started with one false accusation to the authorities, which is the harm the CAREN Act targets.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
• Forsyth County, Georgia, 1912: after a lynching, night riders drove out about 1,100 Black residents. White neighbors took over their farms. The county stayed almost entirely white for 75 years.
  • Sundown towns: historian James Loewen documented hundreds, possibly thousands, of towns that kept Black people out by violence or law, often after driving out those already there (see the old laws tracker).
  • Seneca Village, New York, 1857: the city's largest community of Black property owners was taken by eminent domain and razed to build Central Park.
  • Bruce's Beach, California, 1924: a Black-owned beach resort was seized by the city of Manhattan Beach. In 2022 Los Angeles County returned it to the Bruce family's descendants, an early example of returning stolen land.
  • Chavez Ravine, Los Angeles, 1950s: Mexican American neighborhoods were cleared for public housing that was never built; the land became Dodger Stadium.
  • Black farmland: around 1910, Black farmers owned roughly 15 million acres. Most of it is gone. It was lost to violence, to the U.S. Department of Agriculture's discrimination in loans (settled in Pigford v. Glickman, 1999), and to forced sales of “heirs' property” passed down without a will.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
• Oscarville, Georgia: its Black residents were driven out in 1912. The land was later flooded to create Lake Lanier (Buford Dam, 1956).
  • The Great Mississippi Flood, 1927: Black residents were held in levee camps under armed guard and forced to work on the levees, while white residents were evacuated.
  • Vanport, Oregon, 1948: Oregon's largest Black community, built for wartime shipyard workers, was destroyed when a dike broke. Survivors were pushed into Portland's Albina neighborhood, which was later cut up by a freeway and then gentrified.
  • The Lower Ninth Ward, New Orleans, 2005: levee failures during Hurricane Katrina flooded this mostly Black neighborhood. The Road Home rebuilding program based grants on pre-storm home values, so Black homeowners in undervalued neighborhoods got less; the state and HUD settled a lawsuit in 2011. Much of the neighborhood was never rebuilt.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
The Housing Act of 1949 and the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 sent billions of federal dollars to clear “blight,” a label usually given to the same neighborhoods the redlining maps had marked red. Hundreds of thousands of families were displaced, people of color far out of proportion to their numbers. James Baldwin called it “Negro removal.”

The list of Black business districts and neighborhoods cut apart is long: Rondo in St. Paul (I-94), Overtown in Miami (I-95), Tremé in New Orleans (I-10 over Claiborne Avenue), Hayti in Durham, Black Bottom and Paradise Valley in Detroit (I-375), Sweet Auburn in Atlanta, the Hill District in Pittsburgh, the Fillmore in San Francisco, Albina in Portland, and Greenwood in Tulsa a second time.

Some of this is now being undone. The 2021 infrastructure law created a Reconnecting Communities program, Detroit is replacing I-375 with a boulevard, and Minnesota's transportation department apologized for Rondo in 2015.

sections.label: debated
sections.body:
Gentrification is when higher-income, usually whiter residents and investment move into a lower-income neighborhood, raising rents and property values. That it happens, and that many historically Black neighborhoods have changed rapidly, is documented. A 2019 study by the National Community Reinvestment Coalition estimated that gentrification displaced more than 135,000 Black and Hispanic residents from 2000 to 2013, concentrated in cities like Washington, Portland and Seattle.

What's debated is how much gentrification itself pushes people out, as opposed to normal moving. Some economists find that longtime residents of gentrifying areas are not much more likely to move than residents elsewhere. Others find that those who do leave are pushed to poorer neighborhoods, and that rising taxes, evictions and the loss of churches and businesses damage the community even for those who stay.

The link to the CAREN Act is well documented: as neighborhoods change, longtime residents are reported for doing what they've always done. In 2018 a white woman called police on a Black family barbecuing at Oakland's Lake Merritt. In 2019 a new resident's complaint about go-go music in Washington's Shaw neighborhood sparked #DontMuteDC, and the city made go-go its official music.

What helps: community land trusts that keep homes affordable for good, property-tax relief for longtime owners, tenant protections, and “right to return” policies like Portland's N/NE Preference Policy (2015), which gives families pushed out of Albina priority for new affordable housing.

modules.title: Schools: separate, unequal and still divided
modules.short: Laws against reading, Rosenwald schools, Brown and the resistance to it, 38,000 Black educators pushed out, busing's limits, and unequal funding today.
modules.intro: Education has always been both a target and a path to freedom. Enslaved people were forbidden to read; their children built thousands of schools.

sections.h: Forbidden to read, determined to learn
sections.label: documented
sections.body: After Nat Turner's rebellion, Southern states tightened laws against teaching enslaved people to read. After emancipation, freed people built and funded schools themselves, with help from the Freedmen's Bureau. Between 1912 and 1932, Black communities, Booker T. Washington and philanthropist Julius Rosenwald built nearly 5,000 “Rosenwald schools” across the South, with Black families raising much of the money.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) ruled segregated schools unconstitutional; a year later the Court ordered desegregation “with all deliberate speed,” which many states treated as never. The Little Rock Nine needed federal troops in 1957; six-year-old Ruby Bridges needed federal marshals in 1960. Prince Edward County, Virginia, closed its public schools from 1959 to 1964 rather than integrate, while white students attended private “segregation academies.”

sections.h: The educators who were pushed out
sections.label: documented
sections.body: As schools merged, Black schools were usually closed and Black principals and teachers fired or demoted. An estimated 38,000 Black teachers and administrators in 17 Southern and border states lost their jobs between 1954 and 1965. Research today finds that Black students who have even one Black teacher are more likely to graduate and go to college.

sections.h: Busing, and the line at the city limits
sections.label: documented
sections.body: The Supreme Court upheld busing to desegregate within a district in 1971 (Swann). But in Milliken v. Bradley (1974) it barred courts from including mostly white suburbs in Detroit's remedy, so families could avoid desegregation by moving across a district line.

sections.label: debated
sections.body: A 2016 federal report (GAO) found the share of schools that are high-poverty and mostly Black or Hispanic grew from 2000 to 2013; researchers debate how much this reflects housing patterns versus policy choices. Funding gaps are documented: a 2019 EdBuild analysis estimated that districts serving mostly students of color received about $23 billion less a year than mostly white districts serving the same number of students, largely because schools rely on local property taxes.

modules.title: Wealth: built, blocked and taken
modules.short: Why the typical white family has about six times the wealth of the typical Black family: forty acres promised and taken back, a failed bank, New Deal and GI Bill exclusions, redlining, subprime lending, and how to rebuild.
modules.intro: Income is what you earn; wealth is what you own and pass down. Wealth pays for college, starts businesses, survives emergencies and posts bail. The racial wealth gap isn't mainly about what people earn today. It's the inheritance of policy.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: In the Federal Reserve's 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances, the median white household had about $285,000 in wealth, the median Black household about $45,000, and the median Hispanic household about $62,000. Wealth gaps are far larger than income gaps because wealth builds over generations, and so does its absence.

sections.h: Forty acres, promised and taken back
sections.label: documented
sections.body: In January 1865, General Sherman's Special Field Order No. 15 set aside coastal land from South Carolina to Florida for freed families, in plots of up to 40 acres. That fall, President Andrew Johnson ordered most of it returned to former Confederates. The Freedman's Savings Bank, chartered by Congress in 1865, collected the savings of more than 60,000 Black depositors. Mismanaged by its white trustees, it collapsed in 1874, and many depositors lost most of their money.

sections.h: The New Deal left most Black workers out
sections.label: debated
sections.body:
Documented: the Social Security Act (1935) and the Fair Labor Standards Act (1938) excluded agricultural and domestic workers, the jobs most Black workers in the South held at the time. Most Black workers were left out of old-age insurance and minimum-wage protection for years; the exclusions were narrowed in the 1950s.

Debated: why. Historian Ira Katznelson and others argue Southern Democrats in Congress insisted on the exclusions to protect the racial order. Other scholars argue administrative difficulty was the main reason. The effect on Black families is not in dispute.

sections.h: The GI Bill and the suburbs
sections.label: documented
sections.body: After World War II, the GI Bill paid for college and guaranteed home loans for 16 million veterans. Benefits were run by local officials and banks, who largely shut Black veterans out. A 1947 survey of 13 Mississippi cities found that of 3,229 VA-guaranteed home loans, two went to Black veterans. The Federal Housing Administration's underwriting manual recommended racial covenants, and new suburbs such as Levittown refused to sell to Black families. White families built wealth through rising home values; most Black families were shut out of the biggest wealth-building program in U.S. history.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
Redlined neighborhoods were starved of ordinary loans for decades (see the module on place). When credit finally came, much of it was predatory. Before 2008, Black and Latino borrowers were steered into subprime loans even when they qualified for better ones; Countrywide (2011, $335 million) and Wells Fargo (2012, $175 million) settled federal charges over it. Black and Latino families lost a larger share of their wealth in the foreclosure crisis.

The gap continues through appraisals: a 2018 Brookings study found that homes in majority-Black neighborhoods are valued about $48,000 less than similar homes in neighborhoods with few Black residents.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: What builds wealth is ownership: homes, businesses, land and savings that compound. Tools with a record include down-payment assistance, Black-owned banks and community development financial institutions (CDFIs), community land trusts, help resolving “heirs' property” so families keep their land, and “baby bonds” (Connecticut created the first state program in 2021). Evanston, Illinois, began paying housing reparations in 2021. The Learn quests include ways people who have built wealth can help others build it, beyond donating.

modules.title: Banking, insurance and taxes
modules.short: How mortgages, appraisals, insurance, property taxes and access to banks still cost Black and Latino families more today.
modules.intro: The history of wealth is covered in its own module. This one is about today: the ordinary financial systems where race still changes the price.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: In the FDIC's 2021 survey, about 11% of Black households had no bank account, compared with about 2% of white households. Without one, families pay more for check cashing and short-term loans. Black-owned banks and community development credit unions serve many of these neighborhoods; only about 20 Black-owned banks remain.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Black and Latino borrowers pay higher mortgage rates than comparable white borrowers (Bartlett et al., 2022). Lenders have paid large settlements over steering minority borrowers into costlier loans, including Countrywide (2011) and Wells Fargo (2012).

sections.label: debated
sections.body: A 2021 analysis by The Markup of public mortgage data found lenders were about 80% more likely to deny Black applicants than similar white applicants. The lending industry disputed it, noting the public data lacks credit scores. Regulators and researchers continue to debate how much of the gap comes from bias in models versus differences in credit histories that themselves reflect past discrimination.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Homes in Black neighborhoods are appraised lower (see “Is racism over?”). A 2017 investigation by ProPublica and Consumer Reports found some insurers charged car insurance premiums as much as 30% higher in minority neighborhoods than in white neighborhoods with similar accident risk. And a 2022 study found Black and Hispanic homeowners pay about 10–13% more in property taxes than white homeowners with the same tax rate, because assessors overvalue cheaper homes relative to their sale prices.

sections.label: documented

The quests “Bank with the community” and “Teach a money workshop” put this into practice.

modules.title: Environmental racism: who breathes the dirty air
modules.short: Toxic waste, Cancer Alley, Flint, highways and heat: why polluting facilities cluster near Black, Latino and Native communities, and the movement that fought back.
modules.intro: The same maps that show redlining and urban renewal often show where the landfills, refineries and highways went. Pollution is another way place decides health and wealth.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: In 1982, residents of mostly Black Warren County, North Carolina, lay down in the road to stop trucks carrying soil contaminated with PCBs to a new landfill; more than 500 people were arrested. In 1987 the United Church of Christ's report Toxic Wastes and Race found that race was the strongest predictor of where hazardous waste facilities were located in the U.S.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Along about 85 miles of the Mississippi River between Baton Rouge and New Orleans sit well over a hundred petrochemical plants and refineries, many next to Black communities founded by freed people. In 2014 the EPA estimated that census tracts near the Denka chloroprene plant in LaPlace had among the highest cancer risks from air toxics in the country.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: In April 2014, state-appointed managers switched majority-Black Flint, Michigan, to river water without proper corrosion control, and lead leached into homes for more than a year while officials dismissed residents' complaints. The Michigan Civil Rights Commission concluded in 2017 that systemic racism played a role. A settlement of about $626 million was approved in 2021.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: A 2019 study in PNAS found that Black and Hispanic Americans breathe more fine-particle pollution than is caused by their own consumption, while white Americans breathe less. Highways built through Black neighborhoods (see “Burned, flooded and taken”) brought traffic pollution, and formerly redlined areas run hotter in summer (see the module on place).

sections.label: debated
sections.body: Researchers debate why facilities end up near communities of color. Some evidence shows they were deliberately placed where residents had the least political power. Other studies find that, in some places, poorer residents moved in after facilities were built because land and housing became cheap. Both paths lead to the same unequal exposure.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Communities have won by organizing, testing their own air and water, and suing. Federal environmental justice programs expanded under the Justice40 initiative (2021) and were largely rolled back in 2025, so state and local action matters more. Show up at permit hearings; they are often decided by who attends.

modules.title: The fight for the vote
modules.short: How Black Americans won the vote, lost it to poll taxes, tests and terror, won it back in 1965, and are fighting for it again since the Supreme Court weakened the Voting Rights Act in 2013.
modules.intro: The people who decide whether discriminatory 911 calls stay legal are elected. That is why the vote has been fought over so fiercely for 150 years, and why it is the most powerful tool for passing the CAREN Act.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: The 15th Amendment (1870) barred denying the vote because of race. Within a few years, Black voters elected about 2,000 Black officeholders across the South, from sheriffs to state legislators. Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first Black U.S. Senator in 1870. (See the module on Reconstruction.)

sections.h: Taken: poll taxes, tests and terror
sections.label: documented
sections.body:
When Reconstruction ended, Southern states rewrote their constitutions to get around the 15th Amendment without naming race. Mississippi led in 1890 with poll taxes, literacy tests and an “understanding clause” that let white registrars pass whom they chose. Other tools were “grandfather clauses” (struck down in 1915) and all-white primaries (struck down in 1944). Violence enforced the rest: in Ocoee, Florida, in 1920, Black residents who tried to vote were massacred.

The results were stark. In Louisiana, registered Black voters fell from about 130,000 in 1896 to about 1,300 by 1904. At Alabama's 1901 constitutional convention, the convention president said its purpose was to “establish white supremacy in this State.”

sections.h: Won again: Selma and the Voting Rights Act
sections.label: documented
sections.body: Organizers registered voters at the risk of their lives. Medgar Evers was murdered in 1963, and three Freedom Summer workers, James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner, in 1964. On March 7, 1965 (“Bloody Sunday”), state troopers beat marchers, including John Lewis, on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma. Five months later Congress passed the Voting Rights Act. Its Section 5 required states and counties with a history of discrimination to get federal approval before changing voting rules (“preclearance”). The 24th Amendment (1964) and a 1966 Supreme Court ruling ended poll taxes. In Mississippi, Black voter registration rose from about 7% in 1964 to about 60% by 1967.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: In 2013 the Supreme Court struck down the formula that decided which places needed preclearance, which ended preclearance in practice. Texas announced its voter ID law the same day. In 2016 a federal appeals court struck down a 2013 North Carolina law, finding that it targeted Black voters “with almost surgical precision.” A 2019 civil rights report counted about 1,700 polling places closed in formerly covered areas between 2012 and 2018. In 2023, in Allen v. Milligan, the Court did uphold Section 2 of the act and required Alabama to draw a second district where Black voters could elect their choice.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: About 4 million Americans can't vote because of a felony conviction, and Black Americans are disenfranchised at more than three times the rate of others (Sentencing Project). Many of these laws were written after Reconstruction to target crimes officials thought Black people were likelier to commit. In 1985 the Supreme Court struck down part of Alabama's law for that reason (Hunter v. Underwood). In 2018 Florida voters restored voting rights to most people who had finished their sentences; the legislature then required them to pay all fines and fees first.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: District lines can “pack” voters of color into a few districts or “crack” them across many so their votes count for less. The Supreme Court ruled in 2019 that federal courts won't police partisan gerrymanders, but racial gerrymanders can still be challenged under the Voting Rights Act. Local offices matter as much as Congress: district attorneys, sheriffs and city councils decide how police calls are handled.
