modules.title: Mass incarceration and the war on drugs
modules.short: How the U.S. came to lock up more people than any other nation, why Black Americans are imprisoned at about five times the rate of white Americans, and what is starting to change.
modules.intro: A 911 call can be the first step into the criminal legal system. This module shows how big that system became, who it falls on, and the laws behind it.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: About 1.9 million people are held in U.S. prisons, jails and detention centers (Prison Policy Initiative), up from about 300,000 in the early 1970s. No country locks up a larger share of its people. Black Americans are imprisoned in state prisons at nearly five times the rate of white Americans (Sentencing Project, 2021). In 2010, Pew found that about 1 in 9 Black children had a parent behind bars.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: The 13th Amendment's exception, which made convict leasing legal after slavery (see the module on policing), still allows forced labor in prisons. Starting with Colorado in 2018, several states have removed similar exceptions from their own constitutions; others have voted to keep them.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
President Nixon called drug abuse “public enemy number one” in 1971. The Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1986 set the same mandatory minimum sentence for 5 grams of crack as for 500 grams of powder cocaine, a 100-to-1 ratio that fell overwhelmingly on Black defendants. Congress cut the ratio to 18-to-1 in 2010 (Fair Sentencing Act) and made that retroactive in 2018 (First Step Act).

Black and white Americans use marijuana at similar rates, but in 2018 Black people were 3.6 times more likely to be arrested for possessing it (ACLU, 2020).

sections.h: Did the war on drugs aim at Black communities?
sections.label: debated
sections.body:
In a 2016 Harper's article, writer Dan Baum quoted Nixon aide John Ehrlichman as saying, in a 1994 interview, that the administration linked Black people with heroin in order to disrupt their communities. Ehrlichman's family disputes the quote, and he can't confirm it (he died in 1999). Historians agree the drug war's effects fell hardest on Black communities. Whether that was the goal from the start is debated.

The 1994 Crime Bill is debated too. It funded police and prisons and encouraged “three strikes” and truth-in-sentencing laws. Some Black leaders and mayors supported it at the time because of real violence in their communities. Researchers still argue over how much it drove incarceration, since most prisoners are held under state laws.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: A record can follow someone for life: it can bar them from jobs, housing, student aid and, in many states, voting (see the module on the vote). “Ban the box” rules, first adopted by Hawaii in 1998, now delay criminal-history questions in many public and private hiring processes. Since Pennsylvania in 2018, a growing number of states have passed “Clean Slate” laws that automatically seal eligible old records.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Expungement clinics, Clean Slate laws, reentry programs, and alternatives to police for crisis calls (see the module on policing) all reduce the harm. Lawyers and paralegals can make a direct difference: many people eligible to clear a record never do because they don't know how. The quest for this module asks you to help someone do it.

modules.title: Policing and the 911 call
modules.short: From slave patrols and vagrancy laws to the weaponized 911 call, and what the data shows about who gets stopped and hurt.
modules.intro: The CAREN Act is about one specific harm: calling the police on someone because of their race. This module shows where that harm comes from and why a phone call can be dangerous.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: From South Carolina's 1704 law onward, Southern colonies and states organized slave patrols: white men who rode at night, stopped Black people, demanded passes, searched slave quarters and whipped people found without permission. Every white person was expected to help police enslaved people.

sections.label: debated
sections.body: After emancipation, many Southern patrol duties passed to new city police and sheriffs. How direct the line is from patrols to modern policing is debated: Northern departments (Boston 1838, New York 1845) grew mostly from London's model and from controlling immigrants and labor. Historians agree that in the South, the job of controlling Black movement carried over.

sections.h: Black Codes, vagrancy laws and convict leasing
sections.label: documented
sections.body: The 13th Amendment (1865) abolished slavery “except as a punishment for crime.” Southern states immediately passed Black Codes making it a crime for Black people to be unemployed, to walk at night, or to “loiter.” Those arrested were leased to plantations, mines and railroads, often dying at higher rates than under slavery. Convict leasing lasted in Alabama until 1928.

sections.h: An accusation could be a death sentence
sections.label: documented
sections.body: Many lynchings began with an accusation from a white person. In 1955 Carolyn Bryant's account of an encounter in a Mississippi store led to the murder of 14-year-old Emmett Till. (In a 2017 book, historian Timothy Tyson reported that she later admitted parts of her account were untrue; her family disputes this. That detail is debated.) The lesson the CAREN Act builds on is older than any single case: when the person called about is Black, the police response can be deadly.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
In 2018 and 2020, videos showed white callers phoning police about Black people barbecuing (Oakland), waiting in a Starbucks (Philadelphia, where two men were arrested), selling water (San Francisco) and birdwatching (Central Park). San Francisco passed the CAREN Act in 2020, following Oregon's 2019 law and California's AB 1775.

The data backs up the videos. In San Francisco, only about 1% of “suspicious person” calls in the past year led to an arrest, citation or report. The federal Police-Public Contact Survey (2020) found that Black people who had contact with police were nearly three times as likely as white people to experience threats or use of force.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Cities are sending trained responders instead of armed police to many calls. Eugene, Oregon's CAHOOTS program has done so since 1989. A 2022 study in Science Advances found that Denver's STAR program reduced reports of the low-level crimes it targeted. A federal CAREN Act adds the other half: a consequence for using the police as a weapon.

modules.title: Courts: juries, sentences and the death penalty
modules.short: Who sits on juries, how race shapes charges and sentences, the death penalty case where statistics weren't enough, and the cost of not affording bail or a lawyer.
modules.intro: After a 911 call and an arrest comes the courtroom. Each step, from the charge to the jury to the sentence, is a place where discretion can carry bias.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: The Supreme Court struck down laws barring Black jurors in 1880 (Strauder v. West Virginia), but prosecutors kept removing Black jurors with “peremptory” strikes. Batson v. Kentucky (1986) banned race-based strikes, yet they continued: in Flowers v. Mississippi (2019) one prosecutor had struck 41 of 42 Black prospective jurors over six trials of the same man. A 2012 study found that juries drawn from all-white pools convicted Black defendants significantly more often than white defendants; the gap disappeared when the pool included even one Black member.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Prosecutors decide what to charge, and that choice often sets the sentence. A 2014 study of federal cases found that Black men were more likely than similar white men to be charged with offenses carrying mandatory minimums, which explained much of the sentence gap. The U.S. Sentencing Commission found Black men received sentences about 19% longer than similar white men (2017).

sections.label: documented
sections.body: The Supreme Court halted executions in 1972 (Furman v. Georgia), partly over arbitrary and racially skewed sentencing, then allowed them to resume in 1976. In McCleskey v. Kemp (1987) it accepted a study showing that Georgia defendants who killed white victims were far more likely to be sentenced to death than those who killed Black victims, but upheld the sentence because no intent was proven in McCleskey's case. Justice Powell, who wrote the decision, later said it was the one vote he would change.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) guaranteed a lawyer to anyone charged with a felony who can't afford one, but public defenders often carry far more cases than professional standards recommend (National Public Defense Workload Study, 2023). People who can't pay bail stay in jail before trial, which can cost them jobs and homes, and pressures them to plead guilty. Kalief Browder was held at Rikers Island for about three years without trial, much of it in solitary confinement, after being accused at 16 of stealing a backpack; the charges were dropped, and he died by suicide in 2015.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Jury-selection reforms (Washington State's 2018 rule against implicit bias in strikes), fully funded public defense, pretrial release instead of cash bail for low-risk people, and court watching. Lawyers can take pro bono cases; anyone can join a court-watch program.

modules.title: Watched: surveillance of Black and Brown communities
modules.short: COINTELPRO's war on Dr. King and the Black Panthers, the killing of Fred Hampton, surveillance of Muslim neighborhoods, facial recognition errors, and the neighborhood app.
modules.intro: A weaponized 911 call is one person watching another and calling the police. Governments have done the same thing on a much larger scale.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: From 1956 to 1971, the FBI ran a secret program to “expose, disrupt, misdirect, discredit, or otherwise neutralize” political groups, with a heavy focus on civil rights and Black organizations. Wiretaps on Dr. King were approved in 1963, and in 1964 the FBI mailed him an anonymous letter that urged him to kill himself. The program was exposed in 1971 when activists broke into an FBI office in Media, Pennsylvania, and mailed the files to reporters. The Senate's Church Committee investigated in 1975–76.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: On December 4, 1969, Chicago police, working with information from an FBI informant inside the Black Panther Party, raided an apartment before dawn and killed Illinois Panther leader Fred Hampton, 21, in his bed, along with Mark Clark. Nearly all the shots came from police. In 1982 the city, county and federal government paid $1.85 million to settle the survivors' lawsuit.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: The NYPD's “Demographics Unit” mapped and monitored Muslim neighborhoods, mosques and businesses for years; the department later testified it never produced a single terrorism lead, and it was disbanded in 2014. In 2017 an FBI report invented the category “Black identity extremists.” Facial recognition has led to wrongful arrests of Black people, including Robert Williams (2020) and Porcha Woodruff, who was eight months pregnant (2023); a 2019 federal test (NIST) found many algorithms produced more false matches for Black and Asian faces.

sections.label: debated
sections.body: Some departments use software to predict where crime will happen or who will commit it. A RAND evaluation of a Shreveport program found no statistically significant effect on crime, and critics say such systems recycle biased arrest data into more stops in the same neighborhoods. Supporters say better-designed systems can help. The evidence so far is thin.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Neighborhood apps and doorbell cameras have made it easy to report anyone as “suspicious.” In 2016, after complaints that its crime and safety posts were full of racial profiling, Nextdoor changed its reporting form to require details beyond race. That is the same principle as the CAREN Act: being a person of color in a place is not suspicious.

modules.title: Media and image-making
modules.short: From minstrel shows and The Birth of a Nation to “superpredators” and crime news, and the cameras that turned the story around.
modules.intro: How people are shown shapes how they're treated, including who a caller sees as “suspicious.”

sections.label: documented
sections.body: In the 1830s white performer Thomas D. Rice blacked up to play a character he called “Jim Crow,” and minstrel shows became America's most popular entertainment for decades. The character's name later became the name for the whole system of segregation laws. Caricatures sold products for more than a century; the Aunt Jemima brand was only retired in 2020–2021.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: D.W. Griffith's 1915 film portrayed Reconstruction's Black officeholders as menacing and the Ku Klux Klan as heroes. It was screened at the White House. The NAACP protested it nationwide. That November, a new Ku Klux Klan was founded at Stone Mountain, Georgia, and grew to millions of members in the 1920s.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: The 1968 Kerner Commission, appointed after urban uprisings, criticized news organizations for reporting “from the standpoint of a white man's world.” Studies of local TV news have found Black people shown as criminal suspects more often than arrest data would predict. In 1989 five Black and Latino teenagers were convicted in the Central Park jogger case after intense coverage and a full-page newspaper ad calling for the death penalty; they were exonerated in 2002. In 1995 political scientist John DiIulio warned of coming juvenile “superpredators”; the wave never came, and he later expressed regret.

sections.h: How much does coverage change minds?
sections.label: debated
sections.body: Experiments have found that viewers shown a Black suspect in a news story become more supportive of punitive policies than viewers shown a white suspect or none. Researchers debate how large and lasting these effects are outside the lab.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Ida B. Wells used reporting to expose lynching. In 1955 Mamie Till-Mobley insisted on an open casket for her son Emmett, and Jet published the photographs. In 2020, 17-year-old Darnella Frazier recorded George Floyd's murder; she received a special Pulitzer citation in 2021. Many of the 911 calls that led to CAREN laws became known because someone recorded them.

modules.title: Many targets: Latino, Asian, Native and immigrant communities
modules.short: Lynchings of Mexican Americans, Chinese expulsions and Japanese incarceration, anti-Asian violence, missing and murdered Indigenous women, and the moments these communities stood together.
modules.intro: The same machinery of law, mobs and false accusations has been turned on many communities. Seeing the whole picture builds coalitions, and coalitions pass laws.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Historians William Carrigan and Clive Webb documented at least 547 Mexicans lynched in the United States from 1848 to 1928. In January 1918, Texas Rangers, soldiers and local ranchers killed 15 Mexican men and boys at Porvenir, Texas. In Mendez v. Westminster (1947), Mexican American families won a case against school segregation in California, seven years before Brown v. Board. In 1943, servicemen attacked young Mexican Americans in Los Angeles in the “Zoot Suit Riots,” and police arrested the victims. In 2019 a gunman who had posted about a “Hispanic invasion” killed 23 people at an El Paso Walmart. (See also the module on borders.)

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Chinese immigrants were massacred in Los Angeles (1871) and Rock Springs (1885) and expelled from Tacoma (1885). The Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) was the first U.S. law to bar a group by nationality. About 120,000 Japanese Americans, most of them citizens, were incarcerated during World War II. In 1982, Vincent Chin was beaten to death in Detroit by two white autoworkers who blamed Japan for lost jobs; they were sentenced to probation and a $3,000 fine, which sparked a national Asian American civil rights movement. After 9/11, Sikh and South Asian Americans were attacked, starting with the murder of Balbir Singh Sodhi in Arizona days later. From 2020 to 2021, Stop AAPI Hate received more than 10,000 reports of anti-Asian hate incidents, and in March 2021 a gunman killed eight people, six of them Asian women, at Atlanta-area spas.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Native people were not all granted U.S. citizenship until 1924, and Arizona and New Mexico barred Native people from voting until 1948. The federal boarding schools are covered in the module on conquest. Today, American Indian and Alaska Native women face very high rates of violence. A 2018 Urban Indian Health Institute report noted that of 5,712 cases of missing Native women and girls reported to the FBI's crime database in 2016, only 116 were logged in the federal missing persons database. Congress passed Savanna's Act and the Not Invisible Act in 2020 to improve how these cases are tracked and investigated.

sections.label: debated
sections.body: Some analyses of police killings, adjusted for population, put Native Americans at or near the top of any group, followed by Black Americans; others rank them differently. The numbers are uncertain because race is often misrecorded for Native and Latino victims. Japanese American activist Yuri Kochiyama worked alongside Malcolm X and was with him when he was killed. Black, Latino, Asian and Native organizers worked together in the 1960s and 1970s, and the CAREN Act protects all of them.

modules.title: The women who organized the movement
modules.short: Ida B. Wells, Mary Church Terrell, Claudette Colvin, Ella Baker, Septima Clark, Diane Nash, Fannie Lou Hamer, and the women who founded Black Lives Matter.
modules.intro: Black women did much of the organizing behind the movement's best-known moments, often without the microphone.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Ida B. Wells investigated lynchings at the risk of her life. Mary Church Terrell co-founded the National Association of Colored Women (1896) and, at 89, won the lawsuit that desegregated Washington, D.C.'s restaurants (District of Columbia v. John R. Thompson Co., 1953).

sections.label: documented
sections.body: In 1944 Rosa Parks investigated the rape of Recy Taylor for the NAACP, years before her bus protest. Fifteen-year-old Claudette Colvin refused to give up her bus seat in March 1955, nine months before Parks. Colvin and Aurelia Browder were among the plaintiffs in Browder v. Gayle, the case that ended Montgomery's bus segregation. Jo Ann Robinson's Women's Political Council launched the boycott.

sections.label: debated
sections.body: Leaders chose Rosa Parks rather than Claudette Colvin as the face of the boycott, partly because Colvin was a pregnant teenager. Historians and activists still debate “respectability politics”: whether presenting the most sympathetic plaintiffs helped win public support, or excluded people and narrowed whose dignity counted.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Ella Baker built the NAACP's branches, ran the SCLC's first office and guided SNCC. Septima Clark's Citizenship Schools taught thousands of adults to read and pass voter tests. Diane Nash led the Nashville sit-ins and kept the Freedom Rides going in 1961. Fannie Lou Hamer was beaten in a Winona, Mississippi, jail in 1963 for organizing voters. Dorothy Height helped plan the March on Washington, where almost no women were allowed to speak.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Alicia Garza, Patrisse Cullors and Opal Tometi started Black Lives Matter in 2013. The #SayHerName campaign (2014) brought attention to Black women killed by police, such as Breonna Taylor in 2020. Black women are among the most reliable voters in America, and their organizing has decided close elections.

modules.title: Black LGBTQ history
modules.short: Bayard Rustin, who organized the March on Washington, the Harlem Renaissance, Stonewall, James Baldwin, Audre Lorde and Pauli Murray, and the violence facing Black trans women today.
modules.intro: Some of the movement's most important strategists were gay, lesbian or gender-nonconforming, and many were pushed to the side because of it. San Francisco's CAREN Act protects sexual orientation and gender identity too.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Rustin taught Dr. King about Gandhian nonviolence and was the chief organizer of the 1963 March on Washington. Because he was openly gay, and had been arrested in 1953 on a “morals” charge, other leaders kept him out of the spotlight; Senator Strom Thurmond attacked him on the Senate floor weeks before the march. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously in 2013, and California pardoned his 1953 conviction in 2020.

sections.label: debated
sections.body: Many Harlem Renaissance figures, including philosopher Alain Locke and performer Gladys Bentley, lived openly or semi-openly as gay or lesbian. Whether others, such as Langston Hughes, were gay is debated by biographers. James Baldwin wrote openly about gay love in Giovanni's Room (1956), and poet Audre Lorde described herself as a “Black, lesbian, mother, warrior, poet.”

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Pauli Murray's legal writing argued that segregation violated the 14th Amendment, an argument Thurgood Marshall's team drew on for Brown, and later shaped Ruth Bader Ginsburg's sex-discrimination cases. Murray co-founded the National Organization for Women and in 1977 became the first Black woman ordained an Episcopal priest. Murray's private papers describe a lifelong struggle with gender identity.

sections.label: debated
sections.body: The 1969 Stonewall uprising in New York is often credited to Marsha P. Johnson, a Black trans activist, and Sylvia Rivera. Johnson herself said she arrived after the fighting began; witnesses also credit Stormé DeLarverie, a Black butch lesbian. Their activism afterward, including founding a shelter for homeless trans youth, is documented.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Human Rights Campaign tracking of fatal violence against transgender people in the U.S. finds that a majority of the victims are Black trans women. Calls to police about people's gender or sexuality are a form of the harm the CAREN Act targets.

modules.title: Systemic racism: how institutions carry it
modules.short: What “systemic” and “institutional” racism mean, how neutral-sounding rules carry old discrimination forward, why the law usually demands proof of intent, and the honest debate about disparities.
modules.intro: Many people believe racism ended when the laws that named race were repealed, and that what's left is a few bad individuals. Systemic racism means something different: rules and institutions that keep producing unequal results even when no one in them intends to discriminate.
discuss: Can a rule be racist if no one who follows it is?
Which “neutral” rules in our town might carry old discrimination forward?
What evidence would convince a skeptic?

sections.label: documented
sections.body: In 1967 Stokely Carmichael (later Kwame Ture) and political scientist Charles V. Hamilton introduced the term “institutional racism” in Black Power. Their example: when white terrorists bomb a Black church, everyone sees it. When hundreds of Black babies in Birmingham die each year from lack of food, shelter and medical care, that is racism too, but it works through the ordinary operation of institutions, and few people see it.

sections.h: How neutral rules carry history forward
sections.label: documented
sections.body:
• Schools funded by local property taxes inherit the value gaps that redlining created (see “Place” and “Schools”).
  • Credit scores reward a history of borrowing from mainstream banks, which Black families were long denied (see “Banking”).
  • Legacy admissions favor children of alumni at colleges that excluded Black students for generations.
  • Felony disenfranchisement applies to everyone, but falls on communities policed most heavily (see “The vote”).
  • Zoning for large lots and single-family homes keeps out people who couldn't build wealth.

None of these rules mentions race. Each was shaped by, and keeps passing along, decisions that did.

sections.h: Intent versus impact in the law
sections.label: documented
sections.body: In Griggs v. Duke Power (1971) the Supreme Court held that job requirements with a discriminatory effect violate the Civil Rights Act unless they're truly needed for the job (“disparate impact”). But in Washington v. Davis (1976) it held that the Constitution forbids only intentional discrimination. In McCleskey v. Kemp (1987) the Court accepted a study showing that killers of white victims in Georgia were far more likely to be sentenced to death, and upheld the sentence anyway, because McCleskey couldn't prove intent in his own case. Alexander v. Sandoval (2001) barred private lawsuits over disparate impact under Title VI. The Court did uphold disparate-impact claims under the Fair Housing Act in 2015, and a 2025 executive order directed federal agencies to stop using disparate-impact liability. Because intent is hard to prove, much systemic discrimination is legal.

sections.label: debated
sections.body: Economists such as Thomas Sowell and Glenn Loury argue that group differences can come from many causes, such as age, region, family structure, culture and education, and that disparities alone don't prove present-day discrimination. Others answer that many of those “other causes” are themselves results of past discrimination. Both sides can agree on one test: experiments that hold everything else equal and change only race. Those audit studies, in hiring, housing, lending, medicine and more, keep finding discrimination (see “Is racism over?”).

sections.label: documented
sections.body: The other modules trace systemic racism through each institution: government and law (Reconstruction, the vote), police and courts (“Policing,” “Courts,” “Incarceration”), banking (“Banking,” “Wealth”), medicine (“Science,” “Health”), schools, housing (“Place”), the environment, the media and the military. The CAREN Act targets one link in the chain, the moment a private person uses the police as a weapon, but it sits inside all of them.

modules.title: Is racism over? What the evidence shows today
modules.short: Controlled experiments and large data studies from the last 15 years in housing, lending, policing, courts, medicine, child welfare and everyday life, and how to talk with someone who thinks racism is over.
modules.intro: Real progress has been made: the laws that named race are gone, and attitudes have changed. But when researchers test whether people are still treated differently because of race, holding everything else equal, the answer keeps coming back yes.
discuss: Has anyone here experienced one of these situations?
How would you share one of these findings with someone who disagrees, without starting a fight?

sections.label: documented
sections.body: In a 2012 national study for HUD, trained testers who differed only by race contacted landlords and agents; Black homebuyers were told about and shown roughly 17–18% fewer homes than equally qualified white buyers. A 2019 Newsday undercover investigation on Long Island found Black testers were treated unequally in 49% of tests.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: A study of millions of mortgages (Bartlett et al., 2022) found Black and Latino borrowers paid higher interest rates than comparable white borrowers, including with algorithmic lenders. Homes in majority-Black neighborhoods are valued about $48,000 less than similar homes elsewhere (Brookings, 2018). In 2020 a Black couple in Marin City, California, had their home appraised about $500,000 higher after removing family photos and having a white friend pose as the owner; their lawsuit settled in 2023.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: The Stanford Open Policing Project analyzed nearly 100 million traffic stops (2020): Black drivers were stopped more often, the share of Black drivers stopped fell after dark when race is harder to see, and Black and Hispanic drivers were searched on less evidence. The U.S. Sentencing Commission found in 2017 that Black men received federal sentences about 19% longer than similar white men. In Flowers v. Mississippi (2019) the Supreme Court overturned a conviction after a prosecutor struck 41 of 42 Black prospective jurors over six trials.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: A 2019 study in Science found that a widely used algorithm for deciding which patients get extra care underestimated how sick Black patients were, because it used past health spending as a stand-in for need. Fixing it would more than double the number of Black patients flagged for help. (See also “Health” on pain and pulse oximeters.)

sections.label: documented
sections.body: A 2017 study estimated that more than half of Black children (53%) experience a child-protective-services investigation by age 18, compared with 37% of all children. Black students are suspended at much higher rates than white students for similar behavior, according to federal civil rights data.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: On Airbnb, guests with distinctively Black names were about 16% less likely to be accepted than identical guests with white-sounding names (2017). Anti-Black bias is the most common motive in hate crimes reported to the FBI every year. And this site's own data shows how rarely “suspicious person” 911 calls find a crime.

sections.h: Talking with someone who thinks racism is over
sections.label: plan
sections.body:
1. Agree on what's true. Much has changed; say so. The question isn't whether things are better, but whether people are still treated differently.
  2. Lead with experiments, not anecdotes. Audit studies change only race. Ask: “If the résumés were identical, what explains the difference?”
  3. Invite them to check. Every claim here is labeled and sourced. Skepticism is fine; apply it to the evidence.
  4. Share a story, with permission. One person they know matters more than a statistic.
  5. Don't shame. People defend themselves when they feel accused. Talk about systems, not their character.
  6. Give them something to do. A small action, like reading one module, keeps the door open.

modules.title: Equal or better: what the evidence shows
modules.short: Identical résumés, unequal callbacks. Higher unemployment at every education level. And a long record of achievement against every barrier, which is the opposite of what the inferiority myth predicts.
modules.intro: A common defense of today's gaps is that they reflect differences in effort or ability. Researchers have tested that directly, by sending out identical applications and changing only the name or race. This module shows what they found, and what Black Americans achieved while those barriers were in place.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
In a famous 2004 experiment, economists Marianne Bertrand and Sendhil Mullainathan answered job ads in Boston and Chicago with fake résumés. Identical résumés with white-sounding names (like Emily or Greg) got about 50% more callbacks than those with Black-sounding names (like Lakisha or Jamal). A white-sounding name was worth about as much as eight extra years of experience.

It wasn't a one-off. A 2017 analysis of every field experiment of this kind since 1989 found that white applicants received on average about 36% more callbacks than equally qualified Black applicants, with no decline over 25 years. A 2021–2022 study that sent about 83,000 applications to large U.S. companies found the same bias, concentrated in a minority of firms.

Sociologist Devah Pager went further in 2003: she sent real testers to apply for jobs in Milwaukee. White applicants who said they had a criminal record got called back about as often as Black applicants with no record.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Many Black parents tell their children they must be “twice as good to get half as much.” The data backs them up: at every level of education, Black workers have higher unemployment than white workers, and Black college graduates earn less than white college graduates. The gaps persist even when researchers compare people with the same degree, the same field and the same experience.

sections.h: Education: the record and a popular claim
sections.label: debated
sections.body:
Documented: Black women enroll in college at high rates, and Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs), about 3% of U.S. colleges, produce a large share of Black graduates, doctors, lawyers and engineers, according to UNCF. Their alumni include Thurgood Marshall, Martin Luther King Jr., Toni Morrison and Kamala Harris.

Debated: you may see the claim that Black women are “the most educated group in America.” It comes from college enrollment figures. By degrees completed, other groups are higher. The accurate version is still powerful: Black women pursue higher education at very high rates while facing some of the largest pay gaps.

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
In 1858 the U.S. Attorney General ruled that enslaved inventors could not hold patents. Free Black inventors patented anyway. Economist Lisa Cook (now a Federal Reserve governor) showed in 2014 that Black patenting rose after the Civil War and then fell sharply as lynchings, riots and segregation laws spread, with a steep drop after the Tulsa massacre. The innovation was there. Violence suppressed it.

A few of the people who succeeded anyway: Garrett Morgan (an improved traffic signal and a safety hood), Madam C.J. Walker (one of the first American women to become a self-made millionaire), Dr. Charles Drew (large-scale blood banks), and Katherine Johnson (orbital calculations for NASA).

sections.label: belief
sections.body: The claim that racial gaps reflect inborn differences in ability is old. It was the core of the scientific racism in the module on science. In 1996 the American Psychological Association's task force on intelligence found no direct evidence supporting a genetic explanation for the Black-white difference in test scores. The gap on the National Assessment of Educational Progress narrowed considerably from the 1970s to the late 1980s, far too fast for genes, as schools desegregated and resources reached Black students. Average test scores in every group have risen over generations, which shows how much environment matters.

sections.h: What allies can do with this
sections.label: documented
sections.body: Hiring bias is one of the few forms of discrimination that ordinary employees can fix from inside. Blind résumé review, structured interviews with the same questions for every candidate, “fair chance” policies that delay questions about criminal records, and regular audits of who gets interviewed all reduce it. The quest for this module asks you to propose one at your workplace.

modules.title: A world system
modules.short: Britain paying slaveholders, the partition of Africa, genocide in the Congo and Namibia, Nazi lawyers studying American race law, apartheid, and how other nations are reckoning.
modules.intro: American racism was part of a global system of empire. Seeing that system helps explain why the same patterns appear on every continent, and what other countries have tried in order to repair them.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Britain banned the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in most of its colonies in 1833. It paid £20 million in compensation, about 40% of the government's annual budget, to slaveholders, not to the people they had enslaved. The loan raised to pay it was not fully paid off until 2015. France forced Haiti to pay for its own freedom (see the module “Before race”).

sections.label: documented
sections.body: At the Berlin Conference (1884–85), European powers set rules for dividing Africa among themselves, with no Africans present. In King Leopold II's Congo Free State, forced rubber collection brought mass killing, mutilation and famine; estimates of the dead range widely, from about 1 million to 10 million. In German South West Africa (Namibia), German troops killed tens of thousands of Herero and Nama people in 1904–08; Germany acknowledged it as genocide in 2021.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Law professor James Q. Whitman showed in 2017 that Nazi lawyers drafting the 1935 Nuremberg Laws studied American race law, including state bans on interracial marriage, Jim Crow, and race-based immigration and citizenship rules. Some of them found U.S. law harsher than they were prepared to go, for example in its “one drop” definitions of race.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: South Africa's apartheid system (1948–1994) classified every person by race and confined Black South Africans to “homelands.” Police killed 69 protesters at Sharpeville in 1960. A global divestment movement, led in the U.S. by students, churches and the Congressional Black Caucus, pushed Congress to pass sanctions in 1986 over President Reagan's veto. Nelson Mandela was freed in 1990 and elected president in 1994, and a Truth and Reconciliation Commission followed.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Australia's “White Australia” policy restricted non-European immigration from 1901 into the 1970s, and its governments removed Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from their families (the Stolen Generations); Prime Minister Kevin Rudd apologized in 2008. In Canada about 150,000 Indigenous children were sent to residential schools; the Truth and Reconciliation Commission called it cultural genocide in 2015, and Pope Francis apologized in 2022.

sections.label: debated
sections.body: West Germany began paying reparations to Israel and Holocaust survivors in 1952. Caribbean nations (CARICOM) adopted a ten-point reparations plan in 2013. Germany pledged about €1.1 billion in development aid to Namibia in 2021, which many Herero and Nama leaders rejected as inadequate. Whether reparations, apologies and truth commissions repair harm, and in what form, is actively debated. The precedents themselves are documented.

modules.title: How movements won, and the playbook for this one
modules.short: The bus boycott, the legal campaign behind Brown, the sit-ins, Birmingham, Selma and the CAREN Act itself: what actually made them work, turned into a step-by-step plan.
modules.intro: The civil rights movement is often remembered as a few great speeches. The record shows something more useful: years of preparation, training, local organizing, lawsuits, lobbying and economic pressure, carried out by thousands of ordinary people. Every one of those methods can be used to pass a federal CAREN Act.
discuss: Which of these tactics could work in our city right now?
Who in our community already has relationships with our lawmakers?
What would a “Birmingham moment” look like for weaponized 911 calls, and how do we prepare for it?

sections.label: documented
sections.body:
Rosa Parks was not simply tired when she refused to give up her seat on December 1, 1955. She was the secretary of the local NAACP and had trained in organizing at the Highlander Folk School that summer. Jo Ann Robinson and the Women's Political Council had planned a boycott for months; they printed tens of thousands of leaflets overnight. The boycott lasted 381 days, sustained by a carpool system that moved thousands of people a day.

What finally ended bus segregation was a lawsuit, Browder v. Gayle, which the Supreme Court upheld in November 1956. The boycott kept the pressure on and the community united while the case moved through the courts.

sections.h: Brown v. Board: a 20-year legal strategy
sections.label: documented
sections.body: The NAACP's lawyers didn't start with elementary schools. Charles Hamilton Houston and his student Thurgood Marshall first targeted segregated graduate and law schools, where the inequality was easiest to prove: Murray v. Pearson (1936), Gaines (1938), Sweatt v. Painter (1950). Each win built precedent until, in 1954, Brown v. Board of Education struck down “separate but equal.”

sections.label: documented
sections.body: On February 1, 1960, four students from North Carolina A&T sat at a whites-only Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro. Within weeks, sit-ins spread to dozens of cities. In Nashville, students trained for months in James Lawson's nonviolence workshops, role-playing how to absorb insults and blows without striking back. Combined with a downtown boycott, they won desegregated lunch counters by May. That April, Ella Baker helped the students found the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC). Her principle: “Strong people don't need strong leaders.”

sections.h: Birmingham to the Civil Rights Act: crisis, coalition, lobbying
sections.label: documented
sections.body:
In spring 1963, Birmingham organizers combined marches, a boycott of downtown stores, and the Children's Crusade. Televised images of police dogs and fire hoses turned on children forced a national reckoning. On June 11, President Kennedy proposed a civil rights bill. The March on Washington that August drew about 250,000 people.

The bill still had to get through Congress. The Leadership Conference on Civil Rights coordinated churches, unions and civic groups to lobby every senator, and NAACP lobbyist Clarence Mitchell was so constant a presence he was called “the 101st senator.” The Senate broke a filibuster on June 10, 1964, and President Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act on July 2.

sections.h: Selma: years of local organizing first
sections.label: documented
sections.body: Bloody Sunday in 1965 looked sudden. It wasn't. SNCC organizers had been working in Selma since 1963, running voter registration drives and building trust family by family. Freedom Summer in 1964 brought about 1,000 volunteers, most of them white college students, to Mississippi, and Fannie Lou Hamer's Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party challenged the all-white delegation at the 1964 Democratic convention on national television. (See the module on the vote.)

sections.label: debated
sections.body: Historians and political scientists still argue about which tactics moved public opinion. A 2020 study by Omar Wasow found that nonviolent protests in the 1960s increased support for civil rights, while protests that turned violent pushed some white voters toward “law and order” candidates in 1968. Others argue that the threat of more militant groups and armed self-defense (such as the Deacons for Defense) made officials more willing to deal with nonviolent leaders. Most agree that discipline, clear demands and broad public sympathy were essential.

sections.h: Recent wins this campaign can copy
sections.label: documented
sections.body: San Francisco's CAREN Act went from introduction to a unanimous vote in about three months in 2020. Oregon's law passed in 2019 because a state lawmaker, Janelle Bynum, had police called on her while canvassing and told her story. “Ban the box” spread city by city before states adopted it. In 2018, Florida voters restored voting rights to more than a million people through a citizen ballot initiative that won 64.6% of the vote. The pattern: start local, tell real stories, then go statewide and national.

sections.h: The playbook for a federal CAREN Act
sections.label: plan
sections.body:
1. Map the power. Who decides? The House and Senate Judiciary Committees hear the bill; your own members vote on it. The map's allies layer shows them. (Quest: Map who decides.)
  2. Win locally first. City council resolutions and state bills create precedent and show Congress a wave. (Quest: Win a local resolution.)
  3. Build an unlikely coalition. Churches, unions, civil rights groups, Asian American, Latino and Native groups, and businesses that don't want their customers harassed. (Quest: Build a coalition.)
  4. Tell stories, backed by data. Personal stories move lawmakers; the 911-outcome and BJS data protect the stories from being dismissed.
  5. Go inside and outside at once. Meetings with staff and testimony at hearings, plus public pressure: calls, op-eds, events.
  6. Train people and keep going. Teach-ins turn learners into organizers. Most wins take years, not weeks.

modules.short: What has actually worked, and where you fit in.
modules.intro: None of this history was inevitable, and none of it is permanent. Each of these remedies has a track record, and each has a role for you.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: San Francisco's CAREN Act, Oregon's 2019 law and California's AB 1775 give targets a remedy. A federal version would extend that everywhere. Read and improve the draft, then ask your lawmakers to introduce it.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Programs like CAHOOTS (Eugene) and STAR (Denver) send medics and counselors to calls that don't need police. Ask your city council whether yours has one.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Truth commissions (South Africa 1996, Greensboro 2004–2006, Canada 2008–2015) and memorials like EJI's National Memorial for Peace and Justice in Montgomery put the record where everyone can see it. Teaching these modules is part of that work.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: The Civil Liberties Act of 1988 apologized and paid $20,000 to each surviving Japanese American who had been incarcerated. North Carolina and Virginia have compensated sterilization survivors. Evanston, Illinois, began housing reparations in 2021, California's Reparations Task Force issued its final report in 2023, and H.R. 40 would create a federal commission. Whether and how to do more is debated; the precedents are documented.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: Segregation-era language still sits in some codes and deeds. Volunteers can verify old laws and deliver repeal requests, and many states now let homeowners strike covenants from their deeds.

sections.label: documented
sections.body: District attorneys, sheriffs and city councils decide how the police are used, and they are often elected by a few thousand votes. Register, check your registration, and vote in local elections.

threeThings.h: Race was made by law, recently, and law can unmake it.
threeThings.p: Modern race was written into law between 1450 and 1700 to justify taking land and labor. Segregation, redlining and Tuskegee ended within the lifetimes of people alive today. None of it is natural or ancient, so none of it is permanent.

threeThings.h: The gaps are an inheritance of policy, not a measure of people.
threeThings.p: Wealth was taken (Tulsa, forty acres, the GI Bill), votes were blocked, and identical résumés still get fewer callbacks with Black names. Black Americans built towns, banks and businesses anyway, and many were destroyed for succeeding.

threeThings.h: Ordinary people enforced it, and ordinary people end it.
threeThings.p: Mobs, false accusations and weaponized 911 calls were carried out by everyday people. Everyday people also registered voters in Mississippi, crossed the bridge in Selma, and passed San Francisco's CAREN Act. Each of us decides which side of that history we're on.
